questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT an assumption of perfect competition?

options.text: There are many buyers and many sellers
The product sold is homogeneous
Firms engage in heavy advertising to differentiate their goods
There is free entry into and exit from the industry

questions.explanation: Advertising exists to persuade buyers that one seller's product differs from another's. Under perfect competition the goods are identical and buyers already know every price, so advertising would be pure waste.

distractorRationale.a: Large numbers on both sides are essential, since each participant must be too small to affect price
distractorRationale.b: Homogeneity is what forces a single ruling price
distractorRationale.d: Free entry and exit is what drives long-run profit down to normal profit

questions.stem: The demand curve facing an individual firm under perfect competition is

options.text: a horizontal straight line at the ruling market price
downward sloping from left to right
upward sloping from left to right
a vertical straight line at the firm's chosen output

questions.explanation: The firm can sell any quantity it wishes at the ruling price but nothing at all above it, so the curve it faces is perfectly elastic — a horizontal line. This is exactly what being a price taker means, and it is why average revenue equals marginal revenue.

distractorRationale.b: A downward-sloping firm demand curve belongs to a price maker such as a monopolist
distractorRationale.c: An upward-sloping curve describes supply, not demand
distractorRationale.d: A vertical line would mean the firm sells a fixed quantity whatever the price

questions.stem: In long-run equilibrium under perfect competition, a firm earns

options.text: abnormal profit, because it is efficient
normal profit only, because free entry has removed abnormal profit
no revenue at all
a permanent loss, forcing it to close down

questions.explanation: Abnormal profit attracts new firms, whose extra output raises market supply and pushes price down until only normal profit remains. Normal profit is treated as a cost of production because it is the minimum return needed to keep the entrepreneur in the industry.

distractorRationale.a: Abnormal profit can persist only where entry is blocked, as under monopoly
distractorRationale.c: The firm continues to sell output and earn revenue; it is only the surplus above cost that disappears
distractorRationale.d: Persistent losses would cause exit, which raises price back to the normal-profit level

questions.stem: A price-taking firm faces a market price of ₦150. Its marginal costs for successive units are ₦100, ₦80, ₦60, ₦80, ₦130 and ₦210. How many units should it produce to maximise profit? Give a number only.
questions.explanation: Produce every unit whose marginal cost is below the ₦150 marginal revenue. The fifth unit costs ₦130 and so adds ₦20 to profit, but the sixth costs ₦210 and would destroy ₦60 of profit. Equilibrium output is therefore 5 units.

questions.stem: A perfectly competitive firm making a loss in the short run will continue to produce provided that

options.text: price is above average total cost
price is above average variable cost
price is above marginal cost at every output
total revenue exceeds total fixed cost

questions.explanation: Fixed costs must be paid whether or not the firm produces. So long as price covers average variable cost, each unit sold contributes something towards those unavoidable fixed costs, making the loss smaller than it would be if the firm shut down.

distractorRationale.a: If price were above average total cost the firm would be making a profit, not a loss
distractorRationale.c: Profit maximisation requires price to equal marginal cost at the chosen output, not to exceed it everywhere
distractorRationale.d: The relevant comparison is with variable cost, since fixed cost is incurred either way

questions.stem: Which real-world market comes closest to perfect competition?

options.text: The Nigerian cement industry
The market for mobile telephone networks
A village market where many traders sell identical garri
The supply of piped water in a city

questions.explanation: Many small sellers, an identical product, easy entry with a basin and a scoop, and buyers who can check every price in a few minutes — the garri market satisfies the assumptions more nearly than any of the alternatives.

distractorRationale.a: Cement is dominated by a few very large producers, which makes it an oligopoly
distractorRationale.b: Mobile networks are few in number and heavily branded, again an oligopoly
distractorRationale.d: Piped water supply is a natural monopoly, since duplicating the pipe network would be wasteful

questions.stem: A perfectly competitive firm can increase its total revenue by charging a price slightly above the ruling market price.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: False. Because the product is homogeneous and buyers have perfect knowledge, any buyer facing a higher price simply moves to another seller. The firm loses all its sales, so revenue falls to zero rather than rising.

distractorRationale.a: This assumes some buyer loyalty, which only exists where products are differentiated as in monopolistic competition

questions.stem: Which assumption of perfect competition is most directly responsible for ensuring a single ruling price throughout the market?

options.text: Perfect knowledge of prices by all buyers and sellers
The existence of many firms in the industry
The absence of government interference
Perfect mobility of factors of production

questions.explanation: If every buyer knows what every seller is charging, no seller can hold a higher price and no seller needs to accept a lower one. Perfect knowledge, reinforced by the absence of transport costs, is what collapses all prices into one.

distractorRationale.b: Many firms prevent any one from controlling supply, but numbers alone would not stop price differences if buyers were ignorant
distractorRationale.c: Absence of interference keeps the market free but does not by itself equalise prices
distractorRationale.d: Factor mobility works over the longer term to equalise costs, not to unify the ruling price today

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the assumption of homogenous products in perfect competition?

options.text: All firms produce different goods.
All firms produce the same type of product.
Products are differentiated based on branding.
Firms can set their own prices.

questions.explanation: In perfect competition, the assumption of homogenous products means that all firms produce identical products, making them perfect substitutes for one another. This leads to consumers being indifferent to which firm's product they purchase, as they are all the same.

distractorRationale.a: This option describes a market with differentiated products, not perfect competition.
distractorRationale.c: Branding implies differentiation, which contradicts the homogeneity assumption.
distractorRationale.d: In perfect competition, firms cannot set their own prices; they are price takers.

questions.stem: Why do firms in a perfectly competitive market have no control over the market price?

options.text: There are only a few firms.
They produce unique products.
There are many firms and consumers.
They have large market shares.

questions.explanation: Firms in a perfectly competitive market are price takers because there are many firms and consumers, leading to a situation where no single firm can influence the market price. The large number of competitors means that if one firm tries to raise its price, consumers will simply buy from other firms.

distractorRationale.a: A few firms would suggest an oligopoly or monopoly, not perfect competition.
distractorRationale.b: Unique products would imply some level of market power.
distractorRationale.d: Large market shares would allow firms to influence prices, contrary to the nature of perfect competition.

questions.stem: In the short run, a perfectly competitive firm maximizes its profit when marginal cost equals marginal revenue. If MC is greater than MR, what should the firm do?

options.text: Increase production.
Decrease production.
Maintain current production.
Shut down operations.

questions.explanation: If marginal cost (MC) is greater than marginal revenue (MR), the firm is producing too much and should decrease production to maximize profit. This adjustment will align MC with MR, ensuring the firm operates efficiently.

distractorRationale.a: Increasing production would further increase losses since MC is already greater than MR.
distractorRationale.c: Maintaining current production would not correct the imbalance between MC and MR.
distractorRationale.d: Shutting down is not necessary unless the firm cannot cover its variable costs.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a characteristic of a perfectly competitive market?

options.text: Firms have significant pricing power.
There are barriers to entry.
Firms are price takers.
Products are heavily advertised.

questions.explanation: In a perfectly competitive market, firms are price takers due to the presence of many competitors and identical products. This characteristic ensures that no single firm can influence the market price.

distractorRationale.a: Significant pricing power contradicts the definition of perfect competition.
distractorRationale.b: Perfect competition is characterized by low or no barriers to entry.
distractorRationale.d: Heavy advertising is more common in monopolistic or oligopolistic markets.

questions.stem: What happens to the equilibrium price in a perfectly competitive market when there is an increase in demand?

options.text: It decreases.
It remains the same.
It increases.
It becomes unpredictable.

questions.explanation: In a perfectly competitive market, an increase in demand leads to a higher equilibrium price as consumers are willing to pay more for the same quantity of goods. This price adjustment encourages firms to increase production.

distractorRationale.a: An increase in demand would not cause the price to decrease.
distractorRationale.b: The equilibrium price would change in response to demand shifts.
distractorRationale.d: While price can fluctuate, it typically responds predictably to demand changes.

questions.stem: If a perfectly competitive firm is making a loss in the short run, which of the following is true?

options.text: It must shut down immediately.
It will continue to produce if it can cover its variable costs.
It will increase its output to reduce losses.
It has to raise its prices to cover losses.

questions.explanation: A perfectly competitive firm can continue to operate in the short run even if it is making a loss, as long as it can cover its variable costs. This is because the firm can minimize losses by continuing production rather than shutting down.

distractorRationale.a: Shutting down is not necessary unless the firm cannot cover variable costs.
distractorRationale.c: Increasing output would lead to greater losses if prices remain below average costs.
distractorRationale.d: In perfect competition, firms cannot raise prices; they must accept the market price.

questions.stem: In a perfectly competitive market, what is the long-run outcome for firms earning economic profits?

options.text: Firms will exit the market.
New firms will enter the market.
Prices will remain unchanged.
Firms will increase their production capacity.

questions.explanation: In the long run, if firms in a perfectly competitive market are earning economic profits, new firms will be attracted to the market due to the lack of barriers to entry. This entry of new firms will increase supply, ultimately driving down prices until profits are eliminated.

distractorRationale.a: Firms earning profits would not exit; they would attract new entrants.
distractorRationale.c: Prices will change as new firms enter the market.
distractorRationale.d: While firms may increase capacity, the primary outcome is the entry of new firms.

questions.stem: What type of market structure is considered the benchmark for efficiency?

options.text: Monopoly.
Oligopoly.
Perfect competition.
Monopolistic competition.

questions.explanation: Perfect competition is considered the benchmark for efficiency because it leads to optimal allocation of resources, where price equals marginal cost, and firms produce at the lowest average cost in the long run.

distractorRationale.a: A monopoly typically leads to inefficiencies and higher prices.
distractorRationale.b: Oligopolistic markets often result in collusion and higher prices.
distractorRationale.d: Monopolistic competition allows for some price setting, leading to inefficiencies.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about a perfectly competitive firm's demand curve is true?

options.text: It is downward sloping.
It is perfectly elastic.
It is upward sloping.
It is vertical.

questions.explanation: The demand curve for a perfectly competitive firm is perfectly elastic, meaning that the firm can sell any quantity of its product at the market price but cannot sell any at a higher price. This reflects the intense competition and homogeneity of products in the market.

distractorRationale.a: A downward sloping demand curve is characteristic of monopolies, not perfect competition.
distractorRationale.c: An upward sloping demand curve would imply that higher prices lead to higher quantities sold, which is not the case here.
distractorRationale.d: A vertical demand curve indicates no response to price changes, which does not apply to competitive firms.

questions.stem: In perfect competition, what is the relationship between price, marginal cost, and average total cost in the long run?

options.text: Price equals marginal cost, which is less than average total cost.
Price equals marginal cost and average total cost.
Price is greater than marginal cost but less than average total cost.
Price is less than both marginal cost and average total cost.

questions.explanation: In the long run, under perfect competition, the price equals both marginal cost and average total cost. This condition indicates that firms are producing at their most efficient level, earning normal profits with no economic profit.

distractorRationale.a: This situation would indicate losses, which cannot persist in the long run.
distractorRationale.c: This scenario would suggest firms are not maximizing profits.
distractorRationale.d: If price is less than both marginal and average total costs, firms would exit the market.

questions.stem: What is the primary reason a perfectly competitive firm cannot influence the market price?

options.text: It has a monopoly in the market.
It produces a unique product.
It is a price taker in a competitive market.
It has significant market power.

questions.explanation: A perfectly competitive firm is a price taker because it operates in a market with many competitors producing identical products. This means that no single firm can set its own price; it must accept the market price determined by overall supply and demand.

distractorRationale.a: Having a monopoly would imply pricing power, which is the opposite of perfect competition.
distractorRationale.b: Producing a unique product indicates a lack of competition.
distractorRationale.d: Significant market power contradicts the principles of perfect competition.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an assumption of perfect competition?

options.text: Firms sell differentiated products
There are many buyers and sellers
Firms can set their own prices
There are significant barriers to entry

questions.explanation: One of the key assumptions of perfect competition is that there are many buyers and sellers in the market, which ensures that no single firm can influence the market price. This large number of participants leads to a competitive environment where firms are price takers.

distractorRationale.a: Differentiated products are characteristic of monopolistic competition, not perfect competition.
distractorRationale.c: In perfect competition, firms are price takers and cannot set their own prices.
distractorRationale.d: Significant barriers to entry are not consistent with the assumption of perfect competition.

questions.stem: Why do perfectly competitive firms continue to produce in the short run despite incurring losses?

options.text: They can cover their fixed costs
They expect the market price to increase
They can cover their variable costs
They want to drive competitors out of the market

questions.explanation: Perfectly competitive firms will continue to produce in the short run as long as they can cover their variable costs. If the price is above the average variable cost, the firm can minimize losses by continuing to operate.

distractorRationale.a: Covering fixed costs is not the primary reason for continuing production in the short run.
distractorRationale.b: While firms may hope for a price increase, the decision to continue production is based on covering variable costs.
distractorRationale.d: Driving competitors out of the market is not a strategy applicable to perfectly competitive firms.

questions.stem: What is the primary characteristic of price-taking firms in a perfectly competitive market?

options.text: They can influence the market price
They sell unique products
They accept the market price as given
They have a monopoly on their products

questions.explanation: Price-taking firms in a perfectly competitive market accept the market price as given because their individual output is too small to affect the overall market price. This characteristic is essential for the functioning of perfect competition.

distractorRationale.a: Price-taking firms do not have the ability to influence the market price.
distractorRationale.b: Selling unique products is characteristic of monopolistic competition.
distractorRationale.d: Having a monopoly is the opposite of being a price taker in a competitive market.

questions.stem: In a perfectly competitive market, what happens to the equilibrium output when there is an increase in demand?

options.text: Equilibrium output decreases
Equilibrium output remains unchanged
Equilibrium output increases
Equilibrium output becomes unpredictable

questions.explanation: An increase in demand in a perfectly competitive market leads to a higher equilibrium price, which incentivizes firms to increase their output. This results in an increase in the overall market equilibrium output.

distractorRationale.a: An increase in demand would not lead to a decrease in equilibrium output.
distractorRationale.b: Equilibrium output cannot remain unchanged if demand increases.

questions.stem: How does a perfectly competitive firm determine its profit-maximizing output level?

options.text: Where total revenue equals total cost
Where marginal cost equals marginal revenue
Where average total cost is minimized
Where price equals average variable cost

questions.explanation: A perfectly competitive firm maximizes its profit by producing at the level of output where marginal cost equals marginal revenue (MC = MR). This ensures that the firm is not leaving potential profits unearned.

distractorRationale.a: Total revenue equals total cost indicates a break-even point, not a profit-maximizing output.
distractorRationale.c: Minimizing average total cost does not necessarily correlate with profit maximization.
distractorRationale.d: Price equaling average variable cost is not a criterion for profit maximization.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the concept of homogenous products in a perfectly competitive market?

options.text: Products are differentiated by branding
Products are identical and interchangeable
Products are produced by a single firm
Products vary in quality and features

questions.explanation: In a perfectly competitive market, homogenous products are those that are identical and interchangeable, meaning consumers do not prefer one product over another based on brand or quality. This characteristic is crucial for ensuring that firms are price takers.

distractorRationale.a: Differentiated products are characteristic of monopolistic competition.
distractorRationale.c: In perfect competition, many firms produce the same product, not just one.
distractorRationale.d: Variability in quality and features contradicts the idea of homogenous products.

questions.stem: What is the long-run outcome for firms in a perfectly competitive market earning economic profits?

options.text: Firms will exit the market
New firms will enter the market
Firms will reduce output
Firms will increase prices

questions.explanation: In the long run, if firms in a perfectly competitive market are earning economic profits, this will attract new firms to enter the market. This entry will continue until economic profits are eliminated, leading to a new equilibrium.

distractorRationale.a: Firms do not exit the market due to economic profits; they are incentivized to stay.
distractorRationale.c: Firms will not reduce output if they are making profits; they will increase output.
distractorRationale.d: In perfect competition, firms cannot increase prices above the market level.

questions.stem: Which of the following conditions must be met for a firm to achieve equilibrium in a perfectly competitive market?

options.text: Price equals marginal cost
Total revenue exceeds total cost
Average total cost equals average variable cost
Marginal cost exceeds marginal revenue

questions.explanation: For a firm to achieve equilibrium in a perfectly competitive market, it must produce at a level where price equals marginal cost (P = MC). This ensures that the firm is maximizing its profit or minimizing its losses.

distractorRationale.b: While total revenue exceeding total cost indicates profitability, it is not the condition for equilibrium.
distractorRationale.c: This condition is not relevant to the concept of equilibrium in perfect competition.
distractorRationale.d: If marginal cost exceeds marginal revenue, the firm should reduce output to reach equilibrium.

questions.stem: What is the effect of a technological advancement on firms in a perfectly competitive market?

options.text: It increases the cost of production
It leads to a decrease in supply
It enhances productivity and reduces costs
It creates barriers to entry

questions.explanation: Technological advancements typically enhance productivity and reduce costs for firms in a perfectly competitive market. This improvement allows firms to supply more at every price level, leading to an increase in market supply.

distractorRationale.a: Technological advancements usually lower production costs, not increase them.
distractorRationale.b: An increase in productivity generally leads to an increase in supply, not a decrease.
distractorRationale.d: Perfect competition is characterized by low barriers to entry, which technological advancements do not create.

questions.stem: In a perfectly competitive market, firms are said to be price takers because:

options.text: They can set prices above the market level
They sell products that are unique
The market determines the price
They have significant market power

questions.explanation: Firms in a perfectly competitive market are considered price takers because the market determines the price based on the overall supply and demand. Individual firms do not have the ability to influence the market price due to the homogeneity of their products.

distractorRationale.a: Firms cannot set prices above the market level; they must accept the market price.
distractorRationale.b: Selling unique products is characteristic of monopolistic competition, not perfect competition.
distractorRationale.d: Firms in perfect competition have no significant market power.

questions.stem: What happens to the supply curve of a perfectly competitive firm when it experiences a rise in marginal costs?

options.text: The supply curve shifts to the left
The supply curve shifts to the right
The supply curve remains unchanged
The supply curve becomes vertical

questions.explanation: When a perfectly competitive firm experiences a rise in marginal costs, the supply curve shifts to the left. This indicates that at every price level, the firm is willing to supply less output due to higher production costs.

distractorRationale.b: A rise in marginal costs would not lead to an increase in supply; hence the curve does not shift to the right.
distractorRationale.c: The supply curve cannot remain unchanged if costs have risen.
distractorRationale.d: A vertical supply curve is not characteristic of perfectly competitive firms.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why a perfectly competitive firm is considered a price taker?

There are many firms selling identical products.
They can set prices based on their costs.
They have a monopoly over their product.

The interaction of supply and demand.
The cost of production for firms.

distractorRationale.c: While production costs influence supply, they do not directly determine the equilibrium price.
